checklist.title: Verify SetCode Receipt Encoding/Decoding Invariant: Can cross-type receipt spoofing bypass type-prefix validation?
checklist.test_procedure: 1. Identify all code paths that encode and decode receipts with type prefix 0x04 (SetCode). 2. Verify that the decoder strictly validates the receipt body structure matches SetCodeTransaction semantics when the 0x04 prefix is present. 3. Attempt to craft a malformed receipt: encode a FeeMarket receipt body (type 0x02) but prepend it with the SetCode type prefix (0x04). 4. Submit this spoofed receipt through all entry points (P2P sync, RPC eth_getTransactionReceipt, block import). 5. Verify the system rejects the malformed receipt with an appropriate error. 6. Check for any code paths where type prefix validation occurs after deserialization (too late). 7. Verify round-trip consistency: encode a valid SetCode receipt, decode it, re-encode it, and confirm byte-for-byte equality. 8. Test edge cases: empty receipt body, maximum size receipt body, receipt with extra trailing bytes.
checklist.falsification_approach: To falsify this invariant, attempt to: (a) Pass a receipt body through decoding that would be valid for a different transaction type but is prefixed with 0x04. (b) Find any decode path that ignores or loosely validates the type prefix. (c) Identify any state where the receipt type and body become inconsistent after processing.
checklist.notes: Source: PROP-0013, Primary Element: SG-002, Property Type: Invariant. This is a critical encoding/decoding invariant for EIP-7702 SetCode transaction receipts. Cross-type receipt spoofing could lead to consensus failures, incorrect state reconstruction, or exploitation of type-specific processing logic.

checklist.title: Boundary Validation: Are SetCode receipt type prefixes validated at all trust boundaries?
checklist.test_procedure: 1. Map all entry points where receipt data crosses trust boundaries (P2P message handlers, RPC endpoints, block/receipt import paths). 2. For each entry point, verify type prefix validation occurs BEFORE any business logic processing. 3. Verify validation is fail-closed: malformed type prefixes cause immediate rejection. 4. Check for any code paths that accept untrusted receipt data and pass it through without re-validating the type-body consistency. 5. Examine receipt caching mechanisms to ensure cached receipts maintain type integrity. 6. Review any receipt transformation or migration code for type-prefix preservation.
checklist.notes: Source: PROP-0013, Primary Element: SG-002. Complementary boundary check for the encoding invariant. Even if internal code maintains the invariant, untrusted data at boundaries must be validated.

checklist.title: Verify Encode/Decode Roundtrip Invariant: Does decode_receipt(encode_receipt(T, R)) always equal R for all valid transaction types and receipts?
checklist.test_procedure: 1. Identify all valid transaction types (T) supported by the system (e.g., Legacy type 0x00, AccessList type 0x01, FeeMarket/EIP-1559 type 0x02, Blob/EIP-4844 type 0x03, SetCode/EIP-7702 type 0x04). 2. For each transaction type, construct valid receipt objects (R) with varying field combinations including edge cases: empty logs array, maximum number of logs, large bloom filters, different status codes (success=1, failure=0), varying cumulative gas used values. 3. Invoke encode_receipt(T, R) and capture the encoded byte output. 4. Invoke decode_receipt on the encoded output and capture the decoded receipt result. 5. Compare the decoded result with the original receipt R using deep equality checks on ALL fields: status, cumulative_gas_used, logs_bloom, logs (including each log's address, topics, and data). 6. Test boundary conditions: receipts with zero gas used, receipts with maximum cumulative gas (2^64-1), receipts with 256-byte bloom filter edge cases, receipts with empty vs fully populated bloom filters. 7. Test type-specific fields: for Blob transactions verify blob_gas_used and blob_gas_price roundtrip correctly. 8. Test malformed inputs: attempt to decode truncated encodings, encodings with extra trailing bytes, and encodings with invalid RLP structure to verify error handling does not produce partial/corrupted receipts. 9. Verify that different valid encodings of the same logical receipt (if any exist) decode to equivalent receipts. 10. Check for type confusion vulnerabilities: verify a receipt encoded for transaction type A cannot be incorrectly decoded as type B, and vice versa. 11. Fuzz test: generate random valid receipts and verify roundtrip consistency for thousands of iterations.
checklist.falsification_approach: To falsify this invariant, attempt to: (a) Find a valid receipt R where encode then decode produces R' != R. (b) Identify edge cases in field encoding (e.g., leading zeros, maximum values) where information is lost during encoding. (c) Find type combinations where the receipt body format differs subtly between types, causing cross-type confusion. (d) Identify any normalization or canonicalization in encoding that loses information. (e) Test receipts with unusual but valid log structures (empty topics, maximum topic count, large data fields).
checklist.notes: Source: PROP-0014, Primary Element: SG-001, Property Type: Invariant. This invariant is critical for Ethereum consensus as incorrect receipt encoding/decoding could lead to: (1) State divergence between nodes computing different receipt roots, (2) Invalid Merkle proofs for light clients, (3) Transaction execution discrepancies causing consensus splits, (4) Potential double-spend attacks if receipt validation differs between nodes. The encode/decode functions must be perfect inverses for ALL transaction types to maintain network consensus.

checklist.title: Verify Post-Merge Osaka Block Header Invariant: Are difficulty constant and nonce zero-byte requirements enforced?
checklist.test_procedure: 1. Identify all block header validation functions in the Osaka fork implementation, particularly those handling post-merge consensus rules. 2. Locate the expected constant value for the difficulty field in post-merge blocks (typically 0 or a predefined constant per EIP-3675). 3. Verify the difficulty field validation logic: confirm it checks for exact equality with the expected constant, not just a range or inequality check. 4. Verify the nonce field validation logic: confirm it checks for exactly zero bytes (8 bytes of 0x00), not just non-PoW nonce validation. 5. Craft test blocks with the following violations: (a) difficulty set to non-zero value (e.g., 1, MAX_UINT256), (b) difficulty set to a value close to but not equal to the expected constant, (c) nonce with a single non-zero byte, (d) nonce with all non-zero bytes, (e) combination of both difficulty and nonce violations. 6. Submit crafted blocks via P2P block propagation and verify rejection. 7. Submit crafted blocks via Engine API newPayload and verify rejection. 8. Submit crafted blocks via block import (e.g., during sync) and verify rejection. 9. Verify appropriate error messages are returned that clearly indicate the validation failure reason. 10. Test fork transition edge cases: verify blocks at the exact Osaka fork boundary are validated correctly. 11. Verify that pre-Osaka blocks with valid PoW difficulty/nonce are still accepted when processing historical blocks. 12. Check for any bypass paths where block headers might be processed without full validation (e.g., trusted sync, snap sync).
checklist.falsification_approach: To falsify this invariant, attempt to: (a) Find any code path where a block with non-constant difficulty passes validation in post-merge Osaka context. (b) Find any code path where a block with non-zero nonce passes validation in post-merge Osaka context. (c) Identify race conditions during fork transition where old validation rules might be applied to new blocks. (d) Check if any optimization or caching allows blocks to bypass header field validation. (e) Test if the validation differs between different entry points (P2P vs Engine API vs import).
checklist.property_text: In post-merge Osaka fork, the block header difficulty field must be a constant value and the nonce field must be exactly zero bytes. Any block with non-constant difficulty or non-zero nonce must be rejected.
checklist.notes: Source: PROP-0015, Primary Element: SG-004, Property Type: Invariant. This invariant enforces post-merge consensus rules established in EIP-3675 (The Merge) and extended in subsequent forks. Violation could allow invalid blocks to be accepted, potentially leading to: (1) Chain splits between nodes with different validation implementations, (2) Consensus failures if some nodes accept invalid blocks, (3) Potential exploitation of PoW-specific code paths that should be disabled post-merge, (4) State corruption if blocks with invalid headers are processed. The difficulty and nonce fields are legacy PoW artifacts that must be strictly constrained in PoS context to prevent any PoW-related attack vectors.

checklist.title: Verify Post-Merge Osaka Ommers Invariant: Are ommers_hash and ommers tuple emptiness requirements enforced?
checklist.test_procedure: 1. Identify all block validation functions in the Osaka fork implementation that verify ommers/uncles. 2. Locate the EMPTY_OMMER_HASH constant (keccak256 of RLP-encoded empty list: 0x1dcc4de8dec75d7aab85b567b6ccd41ad312451b948a7413f0a142fd40d49347). 3. Verify the ommers_hash field validation: confirm it checks for exact equality with EMPTY_OMMER_HASH, not just non-null or non-zero. 4. Verify the ommers tuple validation: confirm it checks that the ommers list is empty (length == 0), not just that individual ommers are invalid. 5. Craft test blocks with the following violations: (a) ommers_hash set to a different valid hash while ommers tuple is empty (hash mismatch), (b) ommers tuple containing one valid uncle header while ommers_hash equals EMPTY_OMMER_HASH (tuple/hash inconsistency), (c) ommers tuple containing valid uncle headers with correctly computed non-empty ommers_hash (valid pre-merge block structure but invalid post-merge), (d) ommers tuple with invalid/malformed uncle headers, (e) ommers_hash set to zero bytes instead of EMPTY_OMMER_HASH. 6. Submit crafted blocks via P2P block propagation and verify rejection with appropriate error. 7. Submit crafted blocks via Engine API newPayload and verify rejection. 8. Submit crafted blocks via block import during sync and verify rejection. 9. Verify that validation occurs for both the header (ommers_hash) AND the body (ommers tuple) - not just one or the other. 10. Test fork transition: verify blocks at the exact Osaka fork boundary enforce empty ommers. 11. Verify historical pre-merge blocks with valid ommers are still accepted during archive sync. 12. Check for bypass paths: header-only validation, snap sync, light client modes.
checklist.falsification_approach: To falsify this invariant, attempt to: (a) Find any code path where a block with non-EMPTY_OMMER_HASH passes validation in post-merge Osaka context. (b) Find any code path where a block with non-empty ommers tuple passes validation. (c) Identify if header validation and body validation can be performed separately, allowing inconsistent state. (d) Check if the ommers_hash is validated independently of the actual ommers tuple contents. (e) Test if any sync mode (snap, fast, light) bypasses ommers validation. (f) Check for TOCTOU issues where ommers could be modified after validation.
checklist.property_text: In post-merge Osaka fork, the ommers_hash field in the block header must always equal EMPTY_OMMER_HASH, and the ommers tuple in the block body must always be empty. Any block with non-empty ommers must be rejected.
checklist.notes: Source: PROP-0016, Primary Element: SG-005, Property Type: Invariant. This invariant enforces the post-merge deprecation of uncle/ommer blocks as established in EIP-3675. Ommers were a PoW mechanism for rewarding miners who found valid blocks that did not become part of the canonical chain. In PoS, this concept is obsolete. Violation could lead to: (1) Invalid uncle rewards being distributed, (2) State divergence between nodes with different validation, (3) Potential exploitation of uncle-related code paths that should be disabled, (4) Consensus failures if some nodes accept blocks with ommers. The dual validation (hash AND tuple) is critical - validating only the hash could allow a block body with ommers if the hash somehow matched EMPTY_OMMER_HASH through a collision or bug.

checklist.title: Falsify Header Immutability Invariant: Can a frozen Header object be modified after freeze() is called via slotted_freezable?
checklist.test_procedure: 1. Identify the Header class definition and locate the slotted_freezable mechanism implementation (likely a decorator or metaclass). 2. Locate the freeze() method and verify it properly sets an internal immutability flag (e.g., _frozen = True or similar). 3. Enumerate all fields/slots of the Header object that should become immutable after freeze(). 4. For each field, attempt modification after freeze() has been called and verify an appropriate error is raised (e.g., FrozenInstanceError, AttributeError). 5. Test bypass vectors: (a) Direct attribute assignment via obj.field = value, (b) Attempting to exploit __setattr__ override gaps, (c) Slot descriptor manipulation if using __slots__, (d) Calling object.__setattr__(obj, 'field', value) directly to bypass custom __setattr__, (e) Using ctypes or other low-level memory manipulation to modify frozen state. 6. Verify that all mutation methods (if any exist on Header) check frozen state before modification. 7. Test edge cases: (a) Calling freeze() multiple times (should be idempotent or raise error), (b) Attempting modification during freeze() execution (race condition), (c) Subclass field modifications if Header is subclassed, (d) Modifying mutable objects stored in Header fields (e.g., if a field holds a list, can that list be modified?). 8. Verify the _frozen flag itself cannot be modified after freeze() is called. 9. Test serialization/deserialization: if a frozen Header is serialized and deserialized, verify the unfrozen copy can be distinguished from frozen originals. 10. Verify that __delattr__ is also blocked on frozen instances to prevent field deletion.
checklist.falsification_approach: To falsify this invariant, attempt to: (a) Find any code path that modifies a Header field after freeze() without raising an error. (b) Identify gaps in the slotted_freezable implementation where certain access patterns bypass immutability checks. (c) Exploit Python's object model to circumvent __setattr__ protection (e.g., via object.__setattr__, __dict__ manipulation if not using __slots__). (d) Find mutable objects stored in Header fields that can be modified in-place without triggering the immutability check. (e) Identify any methods that modify Header state without going through __setattr__. (f) Test if subclasses can add mutable fields that bypass the freeze mechanism.
checklist.property_text: A Header object must be immutable after freeze() is called via the slotted_freezable mechanism. No field of a frozen Header may be modified. Any attempt to modify a frozen Header must raise an error.
checklist.notes: Source: PROP-0017, Primary Element: SG-004, Property Type: Invariant. This invariant ensures data integrity for Header objects which are likely critical blockchain data structures. If a frozen Header could be modified, it could lead to: (1) Inconsistent header data being used in different parts of the codebase, (2) Hash mismatches if headers are modified after their hash was computed, (3) Potential consensus issues if header data changes unexpectedly, (4) Cache invalidation problems if cached headers are mutated. The slotted_freezable mechanism suggests Python's __slots__ is being used for memory efficiency, which also affects how attribute access works. Internal bug exploitability classification indicates this is primarily a code correctness issue rather than an externally exploitable attack vector, but could have security implications if exploited through internal code paths.
